summary: For 5–6 year olds learning body parts and the five senses (UK Y1 'Animals, including humans'): name and label external body parts, and match each sense to its organ (sight–eyes, hearing–ears, smell–nose, taste–tongue, touch–skin). A strong approach anchors every sense to a first-hand sensory experience using the child's own body, then uses a labelled body figure and sorting activities to consolidate. Keep it external and observational — no internal organs or mechanisms yet.
misconceptions: Thinking we taste with the whole mouth rather than the tongue.
Thinking touch is only in the hands/fingers, not the skin all over the body.
Confusing smell and taste (they work together when eating).
Assuming eyes 'send out' something to see, rather than receiving light (an early seeing misconception — keep simple).
Muddling which organ goes with which sense (e.g. ears for smell).
Overlooking that other animals have these senses too (thinking senses are human-only).

activities.title: All about my body: label and reveal
steps: Look at a friendly child figure and point to each body part on your OWN body as it is named: head, arm, leg, hand, foot.
Say the name of each part aloud as you touch it.
Match each sense to its body part by touching or labelling: eyes for sight, ears for hearing, nose for smell, tongue for taste, skin for touch.
Give a real example out loud for each sense, e.g. 'I see with my eyes', 'I hear with my ears'.
Answer a lift-the-flap style question: 'What do you taste with?' — mainly your tongue.
Touch anywhere on your skin — an arm, a cheek — and say 'My skin feels, all over my body', not just the fingers.
activities.insight: Each external body part has a name, and each of the five senses is linked to a specific body part you can point to on yourself; taste is mainly the tongue and touch is the skin all over the body.

activities.title: First-hand sense play (the real anchor)
steps: Smell something in a jar covered with a cloth or a lid with holes (orange, flower) using only your nose, then name the sense.
Explore a 'feely bag' of textures with your hands and also against your arm or cheek to show skin feels all over.
Go on a listening walk and name the sounds you hear with your ears.
Taste a tiny piece of food and notice what your tongue tells you.
After each activity, say which sense you used and which body part did the work.
activities.insight: The senses are real, first-hand experiences of your own body; doing them is intended to make the organ–sense link stick.

activities.title: Senses in action: sort objects by sense
steps: Look at real objects or pictures (a bell, a cookie, an ice cube, a flower) and decide which sense tells you about each.
Drag or place each object next to the correct sense organ (bell → ears, cookie smell → nose, ice cube → skin/touch).
Drag or place name labels onto the correct parts of a body outline.
Say a short sentence for each match, e.g. 'The bell is for hearing — I use my ears'.
activities.insight: The sense→organ mapping applies to real objects and situations, not just to naming parts in isolation.

checkQuestion: You walk into the kitchen and you can smell cookies baking, then the oven timer beeps and you hear it. Which part of your body did you use to smell the cookies, and which to hear the beep? And when you touch the warm tray to see if it's hot — is it only your fingers that can feel, or can other parts of you feel too?
checkAnswer: The nose smells the cookies and the ears hear the beep. Feeling is done by the skin, which covers the whole body — not just the fingers — so any bit of skin (an arm, a cheek) can feel warmth or touch.
